title: How to Get Oil Out of Concrete: Old Stains and Garage Floors
metaDescription: Get oil out of concrete with a covered poultice left 24 to 48 hours and repeated, or an enzyme cleaner kept damp 1 to 3 weeks. Garage floor steps.
h1: How to Get Oil Out of Concrete
keyword: how to get oil out of concrete
keywords: how to remove oil from concrete
how to clean oil off concrete
how to get oil stains out of concrete
best way to clean oil off concrete
how to get oil spots off of concrete floor
how to remove soaked in oil from concrete
intro:
To get oil out of concrete, you have to reach below the surface: lay a diatomaceous earth poultice under plastic for 24 to 48 hours and repeat it until the stain stops fading, or apply an enzyme cleaner and keep it damp for one to three weeks. Scrubbing alone only cleans the top, which is why old stains keep coming back.

This guide is about concrete in general: garage floors, basement and shop slabs, sidewalks, patios and old driveway stains that have had months or years to soak in. It explains why oil hides in concrete, how to gauge the depth of a stain, how to mix and apply a poultice, when enzymes beat a poultice, how heat helps, and the order to work in when a whole garage floor is stained.
quickAnswer: Degrease the surface and let it dry for a day to see what is really left. For stains that remain, spread a peanut-butter-thick poultice of diatomaceous earth and degreaser a quarter inch deep, cover it with plastic for 24 to 48 hours, then scrape and repeat. For years-old halos, use an enzyme cleaner kept damp while the concrete is above about 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

sections.heading: How to Get Oil Out of Concrete: The Short Answer
sections.body:
Clean the top, check for a sealer, then use a method that works below the surface.

| Step | What you need | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Degrease the surface | Broom, alkaline degreaser, stiff brush, hose | One scrub, then a day to dry |
| Check for a sealer | A few drops of water | Under a minute |
| Mix a poultice | Diatomaceous earth, water-based degreaser, bucket | A few minutes |
| Apply and cover | Putty knife, plastic sheet, tape | 24 to 48 hours |
| Scrape, rinse, judge dry | Plastic putty knife, hose | A day of drying per round; 3 to 5 rounds for old garage stains |
| Switch to enzymes for old halos | Enzyme cleaner, brush, mister or plastic | 1 to 3 weeks, kept damp |

A fresh spill on a driveway is a faster, different job, especially on blacktop; our guide on [how to remove oil stains from a driveway](/how-to-remove-oil-stains-from-driveway/) covers it. This page is for oil that has already soaked in.

sections.heading: Why Does the Oil Stain Come Back After You Scrub It?
sections.body:
Concrete looks solid, but it is full of capillary pores, tiny channels left as water evaporated from the mix while it cured. Oil travels through those channels the way coffee climbs a paper towel, moving down and outward at the same time. The dark halo around an old stain is oil that has spread sideways under the surface.

### What a degreaser actually reaches

A degreaser emulsifies only the oil it touches during a 10-minute dwell, and the rinse carries that portion off. Most of an old stain sits deeper. As the slab dries, oil from below wicks up toward the drier surface and the mark returns, sometimes nearly as dark as before. It never really left.

### Smooth versus worn concrete

A smooth, troweled garage floor slows oil migration. A worn slab that has lost its top cream layer, like an old driveway or sidewalk, lets oil move faster and deeper.

### What the methods that work have in common

Each one deals with depth. A poultice draws oil upward over many hours. Enzyme and microbial cleaners convert oil to carbon dioxide and water where it sits. Heat thins heavy oil so a cleaner can flush it out. All three are slower than a quick degreaser rinse, and all three reward patience more than elbow grease.

### How clean can an old slab get?

Some very old stains never vanish completely. A slab that has held oil for a decade may keep a faint shadow even after careful work. The realistic goal there is a spot that blends in, no longer feels slick and no longer tracks onto shoes.

sections.heading: How Can You Tell How Deep an Oil Stain Goes?
sections.body:
Clean it, wait a day and look. Anything still dark after a good degreaser scrub is inside the slab.

### Clean the surface first

Sweep, scrub the spot with a strong alkaline degreaser and rinse. That removes dirt and surface film and shows how much of the mark is on top versus inside. Let the slab dry a full day. If the stain is mostly gone, you are done.

### Is the concrete sealed?

Drip water on a clean area next to the stain. If it beads, there is a sealer or coating. If the concrete darkens within a minute, it is bare. Poultices and enzymes only work on bare, porous concrete, because both depend on oil moving through the pores. On a sealed floor, strip that section first.

| Stain profile | Likely depth | Best first method | Typical timeline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dark, still slightly slick | Shallow to moderate | Degreaser, then poultice | 1-3 days |
| Dull, dark, months old | Moderate | Poultice, repeated | 3-7 days |
| Faded halo, years old | Deep | Enzyme cleaner, kept damp | 1-3 weeks |
| Under a sealer or coating | In or below the film | Strip the area first | Varies |
| Gummy residue on top | Surface plus depth | Scrape, hot water, then poultice | 2-5 days |

### Will you coat the floor afterward?

Decide this early. An epoxy coating raises the bar sharply, because coatings fail over oil and often lift at the old stain within a year. If appearance is all you care about, a stain faded to a light shadow may be fine, and a penetrating sealer will keep it from getting worse.

sections.heading: How Do You Make a Poultice to Pull Oil Out of Concrete?
sections.body:
Mix an absorbent powder with an oil-dissolving liquid, spread it on and let it dry slowly under plastic. As the liquid evaporates upward it carries dissolved oil out of the pores and leaves it in the powder. Stone restorers have used the same technique on marble and granite for decades.

### What goes in it?

For the powder, use diatomaceous earth, finely ground clay kitty litter, powdered whiting or, in a pinch, flour. Diatomaceous earth works best because it is extremely porous. For the liquid, a concentrated water-based degreaser suits most stains. Acetone or mineral spirits can tackle very heavy oil on bare concrete, but only with strong ventilation. Stir to the thickness of peanut butter, stiff enough to stay put.

### Are premixed poultices worth it?

Pour-N-Restore is a liquid you pour on and brush in; it dries to a powder that holds the oil. Stone-care brands also sell poultice powders. They cost more than a homemade batch but take the guesswork out of the mix. Our [best oil stain remover for concrete](/best-oil-stain-remover-for-concrete/) roundup compares them.

### How to apply it

1. Start with a clean, dry stain.
2. Dampen the concrete lightly with the same liquid used in the paste.
3. Spread the poultice about a quarter inch thick and an inch past the visible edge.
4. Cover with plastic sheeting, tape the edges and poke a few small holes.
5. Leave it 24 to 48 hours, then uncover and let it dry completely.
6. Lift it with a plastic putty knife, bag it as oily waste, rinse and let the slab dry a day.

### How many rounds?

A moderate stain often loses half its darkness or more on the first round. Keep repeating while it keeps improving; three to five rounds is common on a garage stain built up over years.

### Solvent safety

Acetone and mineral spirits are flammable. Open the garage door, know where the water heater and furnace pilots are, keep solvents away from any flame and wear chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection. A water-based degreaser poultice is slower but removes the fire risk.

sections.heading: Do Enzyme Cleaners Get Old Oil Out of Concrete?
sections.body:
Yes, given time, moisture and warmth. Enzyme and microbial removers do not pull oil out at all. They deliver hydrocarbon-eating microbes plus the enzymes those microbes produce, and over days or weeks they break oil down into carbon dioxide and water inside the pores. Terminator-HSD, a powder mixed with water, is one example; several liquid concentrates target garage and shop floors.

### How to apply one

Clean the surface first so the microbes are not competing with dirt. Mix and apply as the label directs, brush it in and keep the area damp by misting or covering with plastic, especially indoors where air is dry. Do not rinse for at least as long as the label says, often a day or more. Owners commonly report a stain that looks unchanged for several days and then fades noticeably over the following week.

### Why cold weather stalls it

Microbes slow sharply in the cold, and most labels suggest concrete above roughly 50 degrees Fahrenheit. In an unheated garage in winter, a poultice is the better bet. Keep bleach, acid and disinfectants off the area before and during treatment, and rinse earlier degreaser away thoroughly, because all of these can kill the microbes.

### Enzymes or a poultice?

Enzymes win on large, faded stains that would eat up a lot of poultice, and around plants, pets and children where you want to avoid solvents. A poultice wins on speed. If the floor must be ready to coat by the weekend, start with a poultice.

sections.heading: Does Hot Water or a Pressure Washer Get Oil Out of Concrete?
sections.body:
Heat helps a lot; cold water alone mostly does not. Oil thins as it warms and lets go of the pores more easily, which is why commercial crews use hot water pressure washers on fuel station aprons and shop floors.

### Adding heat without a hot water machine

Pour kettle-hot water over the stain and apply degreaser while the concrete is still warm, then scrub and rinse. Or work on a sunny afternoon once the slab has heated up, misting the cleaner so it never dries. Some owners warm a stain with a heat gun on a moderate setting before laying a poultice; keep it moving, because rapid heating can make concrete spall.

### What a cold water pressure washer can do

It rarely removes old oil by itself, but it makes an excellent rinse after a degreaser or poultice. Use a 15 or 25 degree tip held 8 to 12 inches from the concrete. On large areas, a rotating surface cleaner leaves an even finish without wand stripes; see our guide to the [best surface cleaner for a pressure washer](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/).

### When to rent a hot water unit

For a garage floor with years of buildup, renting a hot water pressure washer from an equipment rental shop for a day can be the most efficient route. Combined with a degreaser and a wet vacuum to collect the wash water, it treats the whole floor in one session.

### Sidewalks and patios without damage

On a sidewalk or patio, use the same poultice or enzyme methods and keep the pressure washer tip wide and moving. Avoid muriatic acid, which etches the surface and leaves a bright ring around an unchanged stain, and skip wire brushes on decorative finishes.

sections.heading: How Do You Get Oil Off a Whole Garage Floor?
sections.body:
Degrease the entire floor first, then treat the stains that survive. A garage floor usually has several stains of different ages plus general grime, and working in sequence saves time and material.

### Day one: clear, scrape and degrease

Move everything out and sweep well. Scrape thick, gummy deposits with a floor scraper or putty knife. Spray a heavy alkaline degreaser over the whole floor with a pump sprayer, scrub with a deck brush or floor machine and pull the rinse water toward the door with a squeegee or wet vacuum.

### Map and treat what is left

After 24 to 48 hours of drying, mark each surviving stain with tape or chalk. Fresh and medium stains get a poultice; large, faded halos get an enzyme treatment. Both can run at once on different spots.

| Timeline | Task |
| --- | --- |
| Day 1 | Sweep, scrape and degrease the whole floor |
| Day 3 | Mark stains, lay poultices or enzyme treatment |
| Days 5-7 | Remove, rinse, reassess, repeat where needed |
| Week 2 and later | Seal or coat once fully dry |

### Where should the wash water go?

Not down the driveway or into the storm drain. Collect it with a wet vacuum, let it stand so the oil separates and take the oily portion to a household hazardous waste drop-off. Used poultice and absorbent can usually go in household trash in small amounts; check local rules.

### When to call a pro

Hire it out when the job outgrows homeowner equipment: a big shop slab with years of buildup, a floor where an old coating must come off across wide areas, or a coating project that calls for grinding. Ask for a written quote naming the cleaning method and whether wash water will be collected.

sections.heading: How Do You Know the Concrete Is Ready to Seal or Coat?
sections.body:
Run a water test. Sprinkle water across the treated area and the concrete around it. Clean concrete soaks it up evenly and darkens. If water beads or sits on top of the old stain, oil is still near the surface, nothing will bond there and that spot needs another round.

### Can you paint over a leftover shadow?

Concrete paint or solid stain can hide a faint shadow on an otherwise clean slab, but paint over oil is a common cause of peeling, so pass the water test first. For an even look without a coating, wash the whole floor with a general cleaner; our [best driveway cleaner](/best-driveway-cleaner/) picks work indoors and out and stop treated spots from standing out as lighter patches.

### Which protection to choose

A penetrating silane or siloxane sealer keeps bare concrete looking natural and slows how fast oil soaks in, which buys you time to blot a drip. Exterior slabs are covered in our [concrete driveway sealer reviews](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/). For a garage, an epoxy or polyaspartic coating gives a surface that wipes clean, but follow the maker's prep exactly, which usually means grinding or etching after degreasing; see the [best garage floor epoxy](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/) and [best concrete floor coating](/best-concrete-floor-coating/) guides.

### Fix the leak

A leak that keeps dripping undoes any amount of cleaning. Park over a drip pan or containment mat until the car is repaired, and keep absorbent and degreaser in the garage. A drip handled within an hour takes minutes; one left for a year takes a week of poultices.

mistakes.title: Expecting One Scrub to Fix a Years-Old Stain
mistakes.body: Old oil lives well below the surface, so a single pass of degreaser cleans only the top and the stain reappears as the slab dries. Plan for several poultice rounds or a week or more of enzyme treatment, and compare the dry slab between rounds to track progress.

mistakes.title: Letting the Poultice Dry Too Fast
mistakes.body: A poultice only pulls oil while its liquid is evaporating upward. Left uncovered in sun or wind it can dry within an hour and draw almost nothing. Tape plastic over it, poke a few small holes and leave it a day or two before you scrape it off.

mistakes.title: Killing the Microbes Before They Start
mistakes.body: Enzyme and microbial cleaners contain living organisms. Bleach, acid or a disinfecting cleaner used beforehand stops them, and so does letting the patch dry out. Rinse earlier chemicals away, keep the area damp and work with the concrete above roughly 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

mistakes.title: Coating Over a Stain That Looks Clean
mistakes.body: Epoxy and paint fail over oil even when the stain has faded to almost nothing. If water beads on the spot instead of soaking in, oil is still near the surface. Keep treating until water absorbs evenly, then follow the coating maker prep instructions exactly.

mistakes.title: Using Solvents in a Closed Garage
mistakes.body: Acetone, mineral spirits and lacquer thinner give off flammable vapor that can drift to a water heater or furnace pilot. Raise the garage door, ventilate well and keep ignition sources away, with gloves and eye protection on. With poor airflow, use a water-based poultice or an enzyme product instead.

faqs.q: How do you get oil out of concrete that has soaked in?
faqs.a: Use a method that works below the surface. Spread a poultice of diatomaceous earth and degreaser a quarter inch thick, cover it with plastic for 24 to 48 hours, then scrape and repeat until the stain stops fading. For large, years-old halos, an enzyme cleaner kept damp for one to three weeks usually works better than repeated scrubbing.

faqs.q: Can you get oil completely out of concrete?
faqs.a: Usually, if the stain is recent. Oil that has sat for a few months often clears completely with repeated poultices or an enzyme treatment. Stains soaked into a slab for many years can leave a faint shadow even after careful work, because some oil sits deeper than any method reaches. For those, aim for a spot that blends in and no longer feels slick.

For fresh spills, clay granules such as Oil-Dri or plain non-clumping kitty litter, ground in and left overnight, absorb free oil best. For set-in oil, diatomaceous earth mixed with degreaser into a poultice draws oil up from the pores as it dries. Sawdust, cornmeal, baking soda and flour also absorb oil but hold less of it.

faqs.q: What is the best powder for a concrete oil poultice?
faqs.a: Diatomaceous earth is the strongest common choice because its extreme porosity lets it hold a lot of oil. Finely ground clay kitty litter and powdered whiting cost less and also work well, and flour or cornstarch will do in a pinch. Mix the powder with a degreaser or solvent until it forms a thick paste that stays in place.

faqs.q: How long should an enzyme cleaner stay on concrete?
faqs.a: Follow the label, but most products need a day or more without rinsing and keep working for a week or longer while the area stays damp. Cold slows the microbes, so expect faster results when the concrete is above roughly 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Keep bleach, acid and disinfectants away from the area while the treatment works.

faqs.q: Does Coca-Cola or WD-40 remove oil from concrete?
faqs.a: Not on set-in stains. The mild acid in cola may loosen a little surface grime, but it does not dissolve oil and it leaves a sticky film. WD-40 can free up fresh grease, yet it adds more petroleum to the slab. On old stains, a degreaser poultice or an enzyme cleaner accomplishes far more than either one.

faqs.q: Will a garage floor coating cover oil stains?
faqs.a: Only briefly. Coatings bond poorly to oil-contaminated concrete and commonly bubble or lift over old stains. Coating makers specify a clean, degreased surface before etching or grinding. Keep treating each stain until water soaks into it evenly, then prepare the whole floor exactly as the coating instructions describe before you roll anything on.

bottomLine: Old oil in concrete is a problem of depth, not effort. Clean the surface first so you can see what is really left, then pick a method that reaches underneath: a covered poultice for stains you want gone this week, an enzyme cleaner for big, faded halos you can leave alone for a while, and heat to speed up either. Judge every round on dry concrete, keep going while the stain keeps fading and stop when water soaks in evenly. Then seal or coat the slab and fix the leak so the work lasts.
